Multiple-decrement CoDa model of causes of death (experimental)

Source: R/model-coda.R
coda_causes.Rd

coda_causes() forecasts death rates by cause with the multiple-decrement form of the compositional Lee-Carter model, which Oeppen (2008) proposed and tested on Japanese causes of death. Causes add up to all causes in every draw. The options weights, rho and individual add the extensions of Kjærgaard, Ergemen, Kallestrup-Lamb, Oeppen and Lindahl-Jacobsen (2019). The model is experimental. Status: published, with the deviations listed below; section numbers refer to Oeppen (2008), and to Kjærgaard et al. (2019) for the extensions.

Usage

coda_causes(
  var = "cause",
  total_level = "all",
  jump_off = c("observed", "fitted"),
  residual = "auto",
  rank = 1,
  order = c(0, 1, 1),
  drift = TRUE,
  weights = c("equal", "deaths"),
  rho = NULL,
  individual = FALSE
)

Arguments

var

Stratum variable with the causes.

total_level

Level of var for all causes.

jump_off

"observed" (forecasts start from the observed deaths of the last year) or "fitted" (from the fitted deaths).

residual

Add a residual cause, the part of all-cause mortality not covered by the listed causes: TRUE, FALSE, or "auto" (added when the listed causes leave more than 0.1% of all-cause mortality unexplained in the median cell).

rank

Number of components (1 by default; Oeppen 2008 used 2 for Japan).

order, drift

ARIMA order and drift of each index, as in coda().

weights

Weights of the parts (ages by cause) in the decomposition: "equal" (Oeppen 2008) or "deaths", their mean life-table deaths (Kjærgaard et al. 2019, eq. 10).

rho

NULL (equal weights of the years) or the weight of the last year, a number between 0 and 1: years weighted by rho (1 - rho)^(T - t) (Kjærgaard et al. 2019, eq. 11; they use 0.1).

individual

Add one individual component per cause to the joint components (Kjærgaard et al. 2019, eq. 12).

Value

A model specification.

Details

Model (Sections 3, 6 and 8.3). In each group (the strata that differ only in var, for example one group per sex):

  1. the cause-specific rates m[x, c] add up to all-cause rates m[x], which give life-table deaths d[x] with radix 1 (life_table() conventions); the deaths are split by cause, d[x, c] = d[x] m[x, c] / m[x] (relations of the multiple-decrement life table, eq. 1 and 7);

  2. the array of deaths by age and cause of each year is unfolded into one composition (Section 6), plus the survivors at the upper bound of a closed age range;

  3. the compositions are centred by their closed geometric mean over the years and transformed by the centred log-ratio; the first rank components of a singular value decomposition give sum_j b_j[x, c] k_j[t] (Section 3, steps 1-7);

  4. forecast deaths d[x, c] give all-cause rates from the all-cause life-table deaths d[x] = sum_c d[x, c], and cause-specific rates m[x, c] = m[x] d[x, c] / d[x] (eq. 7, Section 8.3).

The causes add up to the all-cause rates in every draw, and the strata of total_level get their sum. If the listed causes leave part of the all-cause deaths unexplained (residual), that part is a residual cause inside the model and counts towards the all-cause rates; it is not a stratum of the output (package-specific).

Indexes and rank. For Japanese women 1951-1990, Oeppen (2008, Sections 6 and 7) uses two components and selects ARIMA(0,2,2) models for the indexes by AICc; Section 3 notes, for the Lee-Carter model, that one component is usually adequate for advanced economies and that its index can be forecast by a simple ARIMA model such as the random walk with drift. These choices belong to one data set; the defaults here are one component and the index model of coda(), ARIMA(0,1,1) with drift (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, with Oeppen as co-author). rank = 2, order = c(0, 2, 2) gives Oeppen's specification for Japan. With several components, each index has its own ARIMA model, independent of the others (the paper does not say how the second index was forecast).

Deviations from the paper. Oeppen (2008) gives point forecasts only: the jump-off (forecasts start from the observed deaths of the last year, jump_off = "observed") and the draws (bootstrap of the residuals and of the index paths, centred on the point forecast) are those of coda() (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, Appendices B and G). Oeppen (2008, Section 3) replaces zero counts by lightly smoothing the deaths of each year with a penalised histogram smoother whose smoothing parameter is not given; here zero counts are replaced multiplicatively in the composition of each year (Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017, Appendix C, with the package-specific cap 0.5 / z of delta for z zeros in a year; see coda()). How the death rate of the open age interval follows from the forecast deaths is not stated; here the all-cause log rate of an open interval is regressed on the indexes and split by cause through the composition (package-specific, as open = "regression" of coda()).

Draws are expected rates. Predictive draws (mt_forecast(predictive = TRUE)) draw Poisson all-cause deaths given the all-cause rates and exposures and split them multinomially between the causes by the cause shares of the draw, so that the causes also add up to all causes in predictive draws; no other observation noise is added (package-specific).

Weights and individual components (Kjærgaard et al. 2019, Section 2.4). Kjærgaard et al. call the model above CT-CoDA and extend it to the two-step model 2S-CoDA with two elements, weights of the parts and years and cause-specific components. They are options here:

  • weights = "deaths" weights each part (age by cause) by its temporal mean of the life-table deaths, w[x, i] = dbar[x, i] / sum(dbar) (eq. 10), so that a large cause counts more than a small one and splitting a cause does not double its weight;

  • rho weights the years t = 1, ..., T by rho (1 - rho)^(T - t) (eq. 11, after Hyndman, Booth and Yasmeen 2013): the last year gets the weight rho, earlier years less. The paper uses rho = 0.1, chosen by cross-validation (Section 2.8). Eq. (11) states t = 1, ..., T - 1; the text gives the last year the weight rho, which the package follows;

  • with weights, the components are the first ones of a generalized singular value decomposition (van Loan 1976) with these weights of the parts and years: they minimise the sum over parts and years of w[x, i] w[t] times the squared residual of eq. (9). The centre a is the unweighted geometric mean, as in CT-CoDA (Section 2.4: 2S-CoDA "follows the same first steps"). Loadings have unit length; the index of each year is the weighted least-squares fit of that year;

  • individual = TRUE adds the cause-specific components of eq. (12): the residuals of each cause after the joint components (rank of them; the paper uses one) get the first component of their own unweighted SVD, b_i[x] k_i[t], as the paper names it for this step (Section 2.4); the weights of eq. (10) and (11) apply to the joint components of eq. (9). This follows the joint and individual components of Lock et al. (2013) in two steps without iteration, as in the paper.

coda_causes(weights = "deaths", rho = 0.1, individual = TRUE) is 2S-CoDA; with jump_off = "fitted", forecasts start from the model, as in eq. (7) of the paper. rank = 3 is the paper's CT-CoDA (Section 2.8). Every index, joint or individual, has its own ARIMA model of order and drift, independent of the others. The paper selects the order of integration of each index by the augmented Dickey-Fuller test and the ARMA orders by AIC, with a drift for the rank-one indexes (Section 2.8); the settings of the test are not given, and the package uses order. Further choices of the package (reference unknown): in the clr deaths, the individual loadings are centred over all parts, which leaves the closed composition unchanged; the log rate of an open age interval is regressed on the joint indexes only, weighted by the weights of the years; a residual cause gets an individual component, the survivors of a closed age range none. The paper gives point forecasts only. Draws refit the same decomposition (with the same weights of the joint components) to bootstrap samples. With weights of the parts, each cell takes a residual of its own part: pooled resampling (Appendix B of Bergeron-Boucher et al. 2017) would move the large residuals of small, down-weighted parts into the parts that determine the weighted fit, and on mt_example_causes() it about doubled the innovation standard deviation of the refitted index. With weights of the years, the year of each residual is drawn with probability proportional to its weight. mt_parameters() gives the individual loadings and indexes as b_<cause> and k_<cause> with their ARIMA models and the share of the residual variation of the cause after the joint components that they explain (explained_<cause>), the weights w_part and w_time, and the share of the variation of each cause explained by the joint and the individual components (explained_joint, explained_individual; squared Frobenius norms of the centred clr deaths of the cause, Section 3.3.1 and Fig. 4).

The paper replaces zero counts by half a death; zeros here are replaced multiplicatively, as above. The paper's third model, VECM-CoDA (Section 2.5: one SVD per cause and a cointegrated vector error correction model of the cause indexes, with the Johansen test), is not implemented. The paper's data (France, Institut National d'Etudes Démographiques, 1955-2008; the Netherlands, Statistics Netherlands, 1958-2014; 5-year age groups from 25) are not available to the package, so its numbers (Table

  1. are not reproduced. The alpha-transformation that Dong, Shang, Hui and Bruhn (2025) use in place of the clr for compositions of causes with zero counts is not implemented. Compare the model with reconciled() separate models in a backtest before using it.

References

Oeppen J (2008). Coherent forecasting of multiple-decrement life tables: a test using Japanese cause of death data. CODAWORK'08, Universitat de Girona. https://hdl.handle.net/10256/742

Bergeron-Boucher M-P, Canudas-Romo V, Oeppen J, Vaupel JW (2017). Coherent forecasts of mortality with compositional data analysis. Demographic Research 37(17): 527-566. doi:10.4054/DemRes.2017.37.17

Kjærgaard S, Ergemen YE, Kallestrup-Lamb M, Oeppen J, Lindahl-Jacobsen R (2019). Forecasting causes of death by using compositional data analysis: the case of cancer deaths. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C 68(5): 1351-1370. doi:10.1111/rssc.12357

van Loan CF (1976). Generalizing the singular value decomposition. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 13(1): 76-83. doi:10.1137/0713009

Hyndman RJ, Booth H, Yasmeen F (2013). Coherent mortality forecasting: the product-ratio method with functional time series models. Demography 50(1): 261-283. doi:10.1007/s13524-012-0145-5

Lock EF, Hoadley KA, Marron JS, Nobel AB (2013). Joint and individual variation explained (JIVE) for integrated analysis of multiple data types. Annals of Applied Statistics 7(1): 523-542. doi:10.1214/12-AOAS597

Dong Z, Shang HL, Hui F, Bruhn A (2025). A compositional approach to modeling cause-specific mortality with zero counts. Annals of Actuarial Science 19(3): 416-441. doi:10.1017/S1748499524000320

See also

reconciled() with a hierarchy of causes, coda().

Examples

x <- mt_example_causes(years = 2005:2019)
fit <- mt_fit(coda_causes(), x)
fc <- mt_forecast(fit, h = 5, n_draws = 50, seed = 1)
# 2S-CoDA of Kjaergaard et al. (2019): weights and individual components
fit2 <- mt_fit(coda_causes(weights = "deaths", rho = 0.1, individual = TRUE), x)
p <- mt_parameters(fit2)
p[parameter %in% c("explained_joint", "explained_individual")]
#>            stratum            parameter  index      value
#>             <char>               <char> <char>      <num>
#>  1: causes: female      explained_joint    cvd 0.25084751
#>  2: causes: female      explained_joint cancer 0.42160550
#>  3: causes: female      explained_joint  other 0.35442880
#>  4: causes: female explained_individual    cvd 0.16084057
#>  5: causes: female explained_individual cancer 0.09790563
#>  6: causes: female explained_individual  other 0.13299746
#>  7:   causes: male      explained_joint    cvd 0.35871912
#>  8:   causes: male      explained_joint cancer 0.56148267
#>  9:   causes: male      explained_joint  other 0.50032461
#> 10:   causes: male explained_individual    cvd 0.15580499
#> 11:   causes: male explained_individual cancer 0.06960404
#> 12:   causes: male explained_individual  other 0.08919613
